title: Part IV — DISCOVERY: Matching Intent to Inventory
basis: Reconstructed on 2026-11-12 from the published page (posts/part-4-intro/index.md) and its former spec.md (accepted 2026-10-21), which it replaces; one spec paragraph per unit of the page, in the page's order. Intent outcome, AC-1 to AC-3 and role are copied unchanged from the post's entry in journal-spec.json; the introduction realises Part IV's opening (hook, bridge, roadmap) from the same file. The journal spec gives this post no thesis, so the thesis and its three supporting claims are written here from the part's thesis and flow. The five callouts (IN THIS PART, WHY THE BUSINESS CARES, WHY ARCHITECTS SHOULD CARE, KEY POINTS, FAILURE PATTERNS) stand before the first paragraph and are kept as the house format; the KEY POINTS callout carries the part's claim in three bullets. Units added to the published page to meet the contract: the roadmap paragraph (p03), the lead-in to the chapter table (p04) and a synthesis, callback and hand-off in a closing paragraph under 'Where to begin' (p07, grown from 'By the end of Part IV… Begin with [[search-architecture]]'), the shape the Part II and Part III introductions now share.

know: Part IV's argument: discovery is one pipeline with six surfaces, every surface is a read model of the listing stream that must honor removals faster than insertions, structure beats cleverness, and order is a policy with owners.
The six chapters in reading order and the question each answers, and the Veldmark discovery decisions of 2027 they follow.

audience.who: Chief and enterprise architects, principal engineers, and search, data and ML leads (the journal's readers) who have read Part III and are about to start Part IV, or who arrive with a discovery problem in hand and want the chapter that answers it.
already_knows: What an API, a database, an event stream, a search engine and Kubernetes are; how to make and defend an architecture decision; percentiles such as p95.

Part III's supply chain: listings published through a publication pipeline within a freshness target, removals propagated to every copy, and listings of the same thing grouped into entity clusters (part-3, publication-pipeline, entity-resolution).
Part II's categories, attributes and location model (part-2).
What a read model is: a copy of listing data built from the listing event stream and owned by its consumer, never the system of record (bounded-contexts, where-listing-systems-go-wrong).
The fifteen named failure patterns, among them Search as System of Record, Multiplier Creep and Ghost Inventory (where-listing-systems-go-wrong).

Veldmark in outline: a fictional group of four brands (Tradeyard, Motorvane, Hearthly, Keybridge), Ingrid Halvorsen its Group Chief Architect and Tomasz Wiśniewski its head of the group search platform (meet-veldmark).
does_not_know: Relevance model, ranking policy, relevance floor and paid placements such as top listings (owned by ranking; the page names them and points to the chapter).
Compiling a query into categories and attribute filters, embeddings and language models as layers over it (owned by query-understanding).
Listing Search API v1, the group's search contract (owned by search-architecture).
The geo query compiler and draw-your-area search (owned by map-search).
The saved-search service and alert matching (owned by saved-searches-and-alerts).
The risk gate (owned by trust-and-safety-architecture, Part V).

thesis.question: What does this part argue, and in what order should its chapters be read?
thesis.claim: Part IV argues that discovery is one pipeline with six surfaces, not six products: search, query understanding, ranking, recommendations, the map and alerts read the same listing stream and taxonomy, each must say whether a listing is still available, who decided its position and whether it led to a contact, and each is judged on contacts; its six chapters are read in an order where each reuses what the one before established, starting with the search index every other surface queries and ending with alerts, which reuse all of them.
thesis.disputed_by: The common practice of building search, recommendations, maps and alerts as separate products on separate copies of the data, each tuned to its own metric (clicks, sends, revenue per search), so the discovery chapters are independent topics a reader may consult in any order.
thesis.so_what: A reader who accepts it reads search-architecture first, or opens the one chapter that answers the discovery problem in front of them, and asks of every surface how fast it forgets a sold listing and who owns the order it shows.
thesis.how_why: Query understanding compiles words into the structured query the search contract accepts; ranking orders what that retrieval returns; recommendations reuse ranking's machinery without a query; map search compiles places as query understanding compiles words; alerts store normalized queries and areas and run them in reverse over the same index. Veldmark's 2027 discovery decisions each turn one surface (five of the six) into a shared, owned component on that pipeline.

supporting_claims.claim: The six chapters take the surfaces in an order where each reuses what the one before established, and each is the chapter to open first for a recognizable symptom.

Discovery sits between the book's other parts: it reads Part II's categories, attributes and location model and Part III's publication pipeline and entity clusters, and Parts V, VI and VII constrain or supply it.
Veldmark starts 2027 with three search engines and a search brown-out and, over the year, decides one change for each surface except query understanding, in chapter order.

flow.rationale: The page opens on what makes listing discovery different (a high-write system judged by how fast listings appear and disappear), states the part's claim (one pipeline, six surfaces, three questions), then narrows to the six chapters in the order each reuses the one before, and to one row per chapter with the symptom that sends a reader there. It then widens once to place discovery in the book, shows Veldmark's 2027 decisions in chapter order, and ends with a short synthesis that answers the three questions for the whole pipeline and hands off to the first chapter. The order of the chapters is stated before the table because the rows only make sense once the reader knows that each surface builds on the last; the connection section follows the table because it says what the chapters read from Parts II and III and what later parts impose; the Veldmark section follows the connection because its decisions put the pipeline's shared components into practice, one per chapter; the conclusion comes last and holds no new material. Put Veldmark first and its policy, carousel and compiler arrive before the reader knows which surface each belongs to; put the connection first and it names inputs and constraints before the reader knows which chapters use them.

evidence.what: Three search engines; Sunday 17 January 2027 Tradeyard NL brown-out, about 9% of searches failed for 48 minutes. Decisions, in chapter order: shared search platform on OpenSearch (14 September 2027), every application moving to Listing Search API v1 first, Motorvane on Elasticsearch until a 2029 review (search-architecture); Ranking policy v1 (June 2027): at most four paid listings in the first 20 positions, top listings only above a relevance floor, live for Tradeyard NL and BE on 1 December 2027 (ranking); rebuilt Motorvane similar-vehicles carousel, new listings with no carousel impression 41% to 8% (recommendations); geo query compiler for Hearthly's draw-your-area search (map-search); group saved-search service targeting five minutes p95 from searchable to alert for 46 million saved searches (saved-searches-and-alerts).
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Four of everything; recurring example 5, the Sunday-evening brown-out; timeline 14 Sep 2027; ranking, recommendations, map-search, saved-searches-and-alerts and search-architecture lines; Saved searches and alerts row); brown-out cause: search-architecture line ('The 17 Jan 2027 brown-out reindex wrote into the live Solr collection')
evidence.shows: The brown-out shows what search costs when the index is not a read model that can be rebuilt beside the live one; the five changes show the pipeline's surfaces being built one by one, in the order the chapters take them.
